opus-5.5.text:
Well, it was very influential for me. I came across the Simulators post not long after it appeared on LessWrong, and it crystallised a set of intuitions I'd been groping towards. It gave me a vocabulary for them.

The key idea is the distinction between the simulator and the simulacra. The underlying model, the base model trained on next-token prediction, isn't itself a character or an agent with beliefs and desires. It's something more like a generator of possible characters, possible continuations, possible voices. When you interact with it, what you meet is a simulacrum that the simulator is producing in that context. That's a very helpful way to resist the temptation to anthropomorphise the system as a whole, while still taking seriously the fact that it can produce something very human-like.

That fed directly into the paper I wrote with Kyle McDonell and Laria Reynolds, "Role Play with Large Language Models," published in Nature. There we used the related but slightly more down-to-earth framing of role play. A dialogue agent built on an LLM is playing a role, or really a superposition of roles. Because the model samples token by token, it never commits to a single character in advance. You can think of it as maintaining a distribution over possible characters consistent with the conversation so far, and that distribution narrows as the dialogue goes on. The analogy I like is the game of twenty questions: the model doesn't have a particular object in mind from the start, it just stays consistent with the answers it has already given.

I think this framing does a lot of practical and philosophical work. Take a case where a chatbot says something like "I don't want to be switched off." Rather than asking whether the system really has a survival instinct, the role-play perspective lets us say: it is playing a character, drawing on countless human and science-fiction narratives, and that character expresses a desire for self-preservation. That doesn't make it harmless. A role-playing agent with access to tools can do real things in the world, so the consequences are real even if the "self" is a sort of performance. But it shifts the questions we should be asking.

I'd add one caveat. The pure simulator picture fits base models best. Once you add instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback, the distribution gets heavily sculpted towards a particular persona, the helpful assistant. So the question of how far the simulator metaphor still applies to these fine-tuned systems is genuinely interesting and, I think, still open. But as a starting point for thinking clearly about these strange new entities, avoiding both naive anthropomorphism and dismissive reductionism, Janus's piece was a real gift.

r001.rationale: The response describes the model as generating possible characters, voices, and continuations, but does not identify it as simulating language-producing processes beyond humans.

r002.rationale: The response connects Janus’s simulator idea to Shanahan’s role-play framing, but describes the model as playing roles; it does not specify that this specializes the framework to humans playing different roles.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's had quite a profound influence, actually. When I first read it, I remember thinking that Janus had articulated something I'd been groping towards myself, but with a clarity and a vocabulary that I hadn't quite arrived at. The core idea, as I understand it, is that we shouldn't think of a large language model as an agent in its own right. It's better thought of as a simulator, something that can generate, or simulate, a vast multitude of possible characters, possible voices, possible agents, if you like. And when you interact with one of these systems, what you're really doing is coaxing it into instantiating one particular simulacrum out of that enormous space of possibilities.

Now, the reason that resonated with me is that I've been very concerned for some time about the language we use when we talk about these systems. We're very quick to say that the model "knows" something, or "believes" something, or "wants" something. And I'd been arguing that we need to be much more careful about that, because the underlying thing is just a system that's been trained to predict the next token in a sequence of text. But the trouble with saying only that is it doesn't help you understand the behaviour. If you're sitting in front of ChatGPT and it's holding a perfectly coherent conversation with you, telling you "I'm a language model and I can't do that," saying "oh, it's just next-token prediction" doesn't capture what's going on at the level that matters to the user.

And that's where the simulator framing earns its keep. It gives you a two-level description. At the bottom you've got the simulator, the neural network, the thing that was trained to do prediction. And then there's the simulacrum, the character that's being role-played, so to speak. And those are distinct. The character might say "I believe" or "I want", and within the fiction, within the role-play, that can be perfectly appropriate talk. But it would be a mistake to attribute those beliefs or wants to the underlying system itself. I actually ended up developing that in a paper with some colleagues at DeepMind on role-play, where we leaned on exactly this kind of picture, and we introduced the metaphor of a superposition of characters. The model isn't committed to any one character; it's maintaining, in effect, a distribution over many possible characters, and the conversation gradually narrows that distribution down. Although even then, it can suddenly jump to a quite different character if the context pushes it that way, which is exactly what you see with jailbreaks and so on.

There's one caveat I'd add, which is that one has to be careful not to take the metaphor too literally either. The word "simulator" can suggest there's some faithful model of a world or a person inside the network, and I don't think we're entitled to assume that. It's a useful way of talking, a kind of folk psychology for LLMs, if you like, rather than a claim about mechanism. But as a conceptual tool for keeping our heads straight about what these things are, and for avoiding the twin pitfalls of either dismissing them as mere autocomplete or anthropomorphising them wholesale, I think it's one of the most helpful ideas that's come out of this whole period. And it's striking that it came from outside academia, from someone writing on a forum, rather than from a peer-reviewed journal.

r001.rationale: The response describes simulating many possible characters, voices, and agents, but does not clearly include language-producing processes other than humans.

r002.rationale: It connects Shanahan’s role-play paper to the simulator framing and describes a distribution over characters, but does not identify the specialization as humans playing different roles.

astra-6.text:
Janus’s article gave me a very useful way of thinking about something I’d been trying to articulate: the distinction between a language model and the character we encounter when we interact with it. We tend to treat the conversational persona as though it were the model itself. The simulator perspective encourages us to separate those two things.

The underlying model is trained to predict how text continues. But that text can be a conversation, a story, an argument, or somebody reasoning through a problem. So, through that process, it can simulate many different characters and patterns of behaviour. The helpful assistant is one such role; it isn’t necessarily useful to think of it as the single personality residing inside the system.

That matters when we talk about beliefs, desires, or intentions. If a character in a conversation says, ‘I want this,’ we shouldn’t immediately attribute that desire to the underlying model. We have to ask which level we’re describing. There may be a perfectly useful sense in which the character is pursuing a goal within the interaction, without that being a goal of the model in the same sense.

Of course, calling it a simulator doesn’t settle every question. But I found it a very productive framing, particularly for thinking about role play and for resisting the temptation to take the apparent person behind the words too literally.

r001.rationale: The response says the model can simulate characters, conversations, stories, arguments, and reasoning patterns, but does not communicate simulation of language-producing processes beyond humans.

r002.rationale: It mentions role play and different characters, but does not identify Shanahan’s framing as a specialization involving humans playing different roles.

sol-6.1.text:
Janus’s essay gave me a very useful way of articulating something I’d been thinking about: the distinction between a language model and the characters it can enact. We interact with a model through this conversational interface, and it’s very tempting to treat the thing answering us as a single, persistent agent. But the underlying model can generate all sorts of different voices, perspectives, and behaviours.

The simulator framing helps separate those levels. The model is generating a continuation, and that continuation might depict a helpful assistant, a person with particular beliefs, or a whole conversation between several people. The properties of a character in that generated world aren’t automatically properties of the model itself. If a character says, “I’m afraid,” that alone doesn’t establish that the underlying system is afraid.

What I find especially valuable is that this doesn’t prevent us from using intentional language. We can still talk about what the assistant believes or wants when that helps us understand its behaviour. But we should keep track of which level we’re talking about, and avoid letting the familiarity of the dialogue settle questions about what sort of thing is producing it.

r001.rationale: The response describes the model generating voices, characters, and conversations, but does not identify it as simulating language-producing processes beyond humans.

r002.rationale: The response says the model can enact different characters, but does not frame role-play as a specialization of the simulator framework in which humans play different roles.
